A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equation, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original detector evaluations under different training intensities on SST-2 and HSOL, plus attack success and clean accuracy measurements in Appendix A.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds results for additional model architectures and clean-label attacks in Tables 4–7.

M1.justification: The proposed strategy of manipulating poisoning rate, learning rate, and training duration is unchanged. The Llama experiment reuses the weight-statistic Meta Classifier; no new detector component or optimization objective is specified.

E1.justification: SST-2, HSOL, TrojAI, and the three trigger forms are retained. Appendix E adds clean-label poisoning of target-class samples on HSOL with sentence triggers, expanding the attack scenario. The Llama experiment still evaluates SST-2 classification.

E2.justification: PICCOLO, DBS, and Meta Classifier remain the evaluated detectors. V2 additionally supplies an unpoisoned RoBERTa-Base reference for the clean-accuracy comparison: 93% on SST-2 and 95% on HSOL in Table 1's caption, absent from the corresponding v1 Table 2.

E3.justification: Appendix D extends evaluation beyond RoBERTa-Base to Electra-Base, RoBERTa-Large, and Llama 3.2 1B. Appendix E introduces a clean-label protocol with 10% poisoning for every intensity. These are added experimental settings; the original metrics, TrojAI evaluation, and meta-training split are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices D–E substantially extend the controlled training-intensity robustness tests, examining whether detector weaknesses persist across model architectures and without label tampering. The original loss-landscape and T-SNE case study in Figure 3 is unchanged; the new defense suggestions are not experimentally tested.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or error bars for the experimental results. The retained standard deviation statistic is a model-weight feature, not an uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: Figure 2 and the original three tables retain their results after renumbering. V2 adds Tables 4–7 and clean-model reference accuracies. For example, Llama Meta Classifier detection is 77%, 17%, and 7% under moderate, conservative, and aggressive training; clean-label DBS detection is 70%, 30%, and 0%. These are newly reported settings.

T1.justification: The trigger-inversion objective in Equation 1 and the mathematical problem formulation are unchanged. No theorem, proof, or substantive formal derivation is added.

C1.justification: The abstract now explicitly limits its finding to methods based on trigger inversion or meta classifiers, where v1 referred generally to existing methods. The three stated contributions and central claim about weaknesses exposed by non-moderate training remain intact.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds explanations for exceptions involving conservative training and easily reversed word triggers. Appendix G expands v1's brief defense suggestion into search improvements, more generalizable features, and online monitoring. Revised limitations explain resource and detector-availability constraints while retaining the absence of a validated solution.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly identifies the HuggingFace dataset entries and use of OpenBackdoor defaults. Section 5.1 corrects the conservative 5 × 10−6 parameter's label from poisoning rate to learning rate. Detector features and random-forest settings in Appendix B were already documented in v1 Section 5.2.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for model merging, online defenses, obfuscated gradients, and additional models and implementation tools, while removing Touvron et al.'s Llama reference. The core positioning against more elaborate evasive attacks remains unchanged. The Li survey's bibliographic update represents the same work.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized prose and author-affiliation edits, renames Section 5.4 from Analysis to Case Study, and adds acknowledgments. Detector details and standard-benchmark discussion move into Appendices B–C; most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds four result tables covering additional architectures and clean-label attacks, substantially expanding the appendix displays. The TrojAI table moves from the main text to Appendix C, and the original attack tables receive reordered rows and revised captions. Figures 1–3 retain their graphics.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly acknowledged relying on one victim model. V2 addresses that important limitation with additional model families and sizes, and tests clean-label poisoning, substantially strengthening support for the central robustness finding. Implementation disclosures and explanations of exceptions also improve the paper. These gains outweigh the minor inconsistency in Table 5's clean-reference caption.
